newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambian international reserves up despite aid cut.
newsitem.headline: Zambian international reserves up despite aid cut.

text.p: Zambia's gross international reserves for December rose to their highest level in over a year despite aid cuts which analysts had predicted would push levels to a record low, the central bank said on Thursday.
Central bank statistics showed gross international reserves rising to $220.66 million in December from $206.57 million in November. The reserves stood at an annual low of $141.52 million in August.
A central bank official attributed the rise to increased buying of convertible currency by the bank.
"The bank has been buying a lot more hard currency from the market than before. That is the main reason for the increase," the official said.

Analysts had forecast a drastic drop in the reserves as western governments cut aid to force President Frederick Chiluba's government to withdraw constitutional amendments they said would limit Zambians' choices in an election held last November.
The amendments, which banned some candidates including former president Kenneth Kaunda from standing, forced seven opposition parties to boycott the polls.
Chiluba's Movement for Multiparty Democracy won the poll by a landslide.
Analysts said the country's reserves had dropped to around three weeks import cover -- well below the three months recommended by multilateral donors by September because of the aid cuts.
They predicted either a continued drop in the reserves or a sharp devalutaion of the local currency as the government tried to accumulate reserves demanded by multilateral donors.
Independent reports forecast a devaluation of 15 percent to around 1,450 and 1,500 kwacha per dollar by the end of the year.
However the kwacha has remained steady at around 1,320 up to mid-January 1997.

Most Western governments have indicated they will maintain aid cuts in 1997, but Chiluba has said his government would not rely on donor funding to meet its financial obligations in 1997 and would instead cut public spending.
